utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Court Deputy, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, this is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we hear the first witness, are there any matters that the parties would like to bring to the attention of this Bench? Well, Mr. Karnavas, do you have the witness here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and we are ready to proceed. And the witness has asked for no protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Examined by Mr. Karnavas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what your name is for the record.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: My name is Ljubisav Simic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you please spell your last name for us.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: S-i-m-i-c.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, where are you from?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long have you lived in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: My family had a property in Srebrenica municipality and in Bratunac. I was born in Srebrenica municipality, and I have resided and completed my elementary school in Bratunac and my high school in Ljubovija. And I went to college in Belgrade. I've worked in Bratunac, which is how it is today. I also reside in Bratunac nowadays.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Ljubovija, that's across the river, across the Drina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. 6 kilometres from our town on the outside of the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please briefly describe to us your educational background.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I have completed high school, focusing on humanities, following which I studied languages at the university in Belgrade. I majored in Yugoslav literature and Serbo-Croatian language. This is what I studied at the time. I also taught this at school, up until the war started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And where did you teach?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I taught at the secondary school centre in Bratunac, which is where I work nowadays as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you said you taught up until the war. Could you please explain to us what your occupation was or what you were doing in general during the war.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I became involved in politics during the first multi-party elections. And I was proposed by a Serbian assemblyman to the position of the president of the municipality, and I held that office for a certain time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Were you the president of the municipality back in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before we speak about the events around July 1995, and in particular prior to and after the fall of Srebrenica, could you please describe for us what exactly that function as president of the municipality encompassed.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: President of municipality up until the last elections when this was changed, was also the president of the local assembly, was in charge of organising the sessions of the assembly, preparing agendas, and the functioning of the assembly, as well as implementation of assembly's decisions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You may need to speak up a little louder.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: The decisions of the assembly were implemented by a collective body which was called the Executive Board. Yes, that's what it was called. It's some kind of local government, this Executive Board. Yes, that's what it was called. There were also other assembly organs in charge of their respective affairs, such as finance, economy, and so on. They also implemented decisions within their scope of authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, we just may need to have you speak a little louder so the interpreters can hear you. And please, if you could speak maybe a little slower too so they can keep up with the translation.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I will try.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Simic, I want to focus your attention to July 1995. Okay.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in particular, I would like us to discuss the events about Srebrenica. Could you please tell us where you were about the time that you heard that Srebrenica had fallen or was about to fall.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I was away on business in Podgorica and Gnjilani. I heard about this while travelling in the car from Podgorica to Gnjilani. I came to the hotel in Gnjilani. It was quite late at night, midnight or 1.00 a.m., and the receptionist, upon seeing my ID and upon seeing where I was from asked me whether I had heard that Srebrenica had fallen. Because of that and because of what I heard while travelling in the car, I called my wife at home to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you learn from your wife?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: She told me that that seemed to be true, it appeared to be true, and that she -- and that Mladic's police came looking for me twice at home. I asked her what she had told them, and I believed that she had given a good answer, saying that I wasn't there. It wasn't clear to the policemen or to General Mladic where I was exactly. I determined this later. I was unable to go back that night because I had to finish the business I had in Gnjilani. We completed that the following morning and then we headed back to Bratunac. We encountered a lot of difficulties of technical nature on our road back. We did not have enough fuel, our car was out of order. It was difficult to find fuel. And we arrived there in the evening in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you arrived in the evening back in Bratunac, could you tell us what did you do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what did you do?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: The whole time from the moment I heard the news, up until I returned back in Bratunac, I felt very uncomfortable and I was anxious as to what I would find upon returning home. I had no details, I didn't know why General Mladic came looking for me, and why I was needed, and this is why I immediately went to the municipal building. I found president of the Executive Board there, and he told me that it seemed that Srebrenica had fallen and that there would be no more fighting, military combat, and that there would be some negotiations in the Fontana Hotel the following morning regarding that. And I was to meet him the following morning at the command at General Mladic's, that there was supposed to be a meeting or something there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can stop you there for a second. The individual that you met that evening, what is his name?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Srbislav Davidovic. He is the president of the Executive Board. He was also, I don't know if I can say, mobilised, but he was a member of the Labour Battalion. And these people were deployed in times of specific danger or specific threat. And he had to go from the municipality to the positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Where his son was as well. That was in Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you indicated that you had been informed that you were to meet with General Mladic the next morning. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us what you did the next morning.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to the suggestion of the president of the Executive Board, I put on a military uniform, as if I held some kind of a military post as well. And I came to the meeting wearing a uniform. So in a way, I would deter Mladic from asking me where I had been. I came to the meeting with the president of the Executive Board. I think he also wore a uniform at the time. I think he did. We came to the office of the Bratunac Brigade. We found Mladic there, together with a couple of other soldiers who I think were on his security detail. We greeted each other. The general asked me: I was unable to see you these past few days. That's what he told me. And I tried to be relaxed and joked about me being on one hill and general being on the other hill so that we missed each other. And in this way, I avoided any further conversation and inquiry as to where I had been. Then we sat down. He ordered coffee for us. And I think we were waiting for somebody else to arrive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I could stop you here for a second. Could you please tell us exactly, could you please tell us exactly, where was the Bratunac Brigade headquarters that you had this meeting or this encounter with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: The staff of the Bratunac Brigade, the headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade from the very beginning was located in the ceramic tile factory on the ground level to the right from the main entrance. That's where that office was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where you met General Mladic, on the ground floor?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. In that office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you were in that office having this conversation with General Mladic, did you ever see Mr. Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: No. No. Definitely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know of him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I did. He was one of brigade commanders who was appointed shortly before that, one of the newer commanders. I couldn't tell you exactly how long before that he was appointed, but we knew of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Had he been in the room at that time, you would have been able to recognise him. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I would not only recognise him, I would also greet him and I would definitely remember that he was present. Perhaps it would have been easier for me had he been there because it would have been easier to defend myself from Mladic's inquiry as to where I had been. Was I clear enough or do I need to explain this further?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine. Now, if I could please tell us what exactly was discussed between you and Mladic and whoever else was there at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: In addition to the president of the Executive Board, Aleksandar Tesic also came, who was in charge of mobilisation, with the office which was within the Ministry of Defence. There was a local priest there who arrived later. I think that Mr. Deronjic was supposed to come as well, but -- although I had heard that he had been invited, to my surprise he didn't come to the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And could you please tell us what was discussed. And incidentally, before you tell us, could you please tell us exactly or to the best of your recollection, about what time in the morning is it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: It could have been between 7.00 and 8.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you please tell us now what was discussed during that meeting that you and the others had with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: The meeting did not impress me as a typical meeting held at the brigade, when we were invited to be briefed about the situation of the brigade, when we needed to be informed about what assistance we needed to provide, be it footwear, cigarettes, food, whatever we were in charge of. So this was more of a conversation-type meeting. I would say that this was an exploratory meeting, where the general wanted to feel our pulse, so to speak, and see what we thought about the new situation. He said that Srebrenica had been defeated, the army had been defeated in Srebrenica, and that following that, we were to have a meeting at the Fontana Hotel. He said that I and president of the Executive Board should attend the meeting, and that it would be an official meeting held at 10.00 in the morning. And since I was not informed of the situation on the ground, I had to conceal that fact. I couldn't show that. I couldn't demonstrate that. And I had to figure out what had actually happened and what problems we encountered. The general gave us a summary description of the situation. So without being physically present there I gathered that the population had left the town of Srebrenica, that the population was gathering in Potocari, in the industrial zone. And Mladic expected us to attend the meeting and to give some proposals to what should be done. Mladic at the time proposed several options about which he claimed he had heard from people in Srebrenica, probably through some officers subordinated to him who had gone there. Some suggested that the population wanted to be evacuated, some suggested that some wanted to remain, and that all these options should be analysed and appropriate solutions found. I did not give any comments to any of the options, except that I said that the option which covered the population remaining there, which I did not oppose at all, I said that we should undertake to protect the population which expressed desire to remain in Srebrenica. I said that because I was afraid of the consequences that would ensue following the conflicts in previous years. I simply did not trust in the ability of local police and the army to protect adequately the remaining population. This is why I insisted with the general that this should be an obligation of his and that we were unable to guarantee that. So that we wouldn't come in a situation where we would blame ourselves for something we weren't able to do. The general listened to the comments. He said that the representatives of civilian government and the army as well as representatives of the Dutch Battalion would be there, that they would give their requests, and that everybody would be able to voice their opinion at the meeting. The meeting started at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you. Before we get to the next meeting - and we have to take a pause occasionally - that first meeting with General Mladic, could you please tell us about how long did it take.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't think it was more than an hour, not even that. Because as I told you, it wasn't a typical meeting. It was a type of brief conversation. That's what it was. I said what I've just described to you. Most of the people agreed with my opinion. They said that they were concerned, that this should be taken care of so that we wouldn't be -- we wouldn't encounter problems that we had encountered at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you go to the next meeting, the one that General Mladic had told you that would take place at 10.00 at the Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. He also added that we were to go home, to take off our uniforms, and that we were to wear our normal work clothes, the clothes that we normally wore when we went to work. And so I did that, and I came back to the meeting which started at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, could you please give us a brief description of what you recall happened at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I will try to tell you everything I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Try and make it brief, though, so we don't go out for too long.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: The residents of Srebrenica were represented by a woman and two men. And there was a representative of the Dutch Battalion. I think he was a commander. I don't really know much about the ranks, but I think he was a senior officer. So somebody from that battalion. Then there was General Krstic; General Mladic; president of the Executive Board, Srbislav Davidovic; myself; Miroslav Deronjic; and some people from the Zvornik police, I think somebody called Vasic. The people from Srebrenica reacted in a very frustrated manner, asking that the evacuation of the population in the direction of Kladanj and Tuzla be organized urgently at any cost. They said that this should not be postponed, that a catastrophe was about to take place there and while we were meeting there, there were things going on there that were not civilised. I'm quoting here the words of the lady who represented the residents of Srebrenica. As I told you, I wasn't there, physically present, but I believed that what she was saying was true. Then General Mladic suggested that the three of them and the representatives of our government, meaning myself and Davidovic, the president of the Executive Board, and perhaps some other persons, should establish a team that would assist in that situation. The three of them were to convey to the citizens gathered in Potocari that there were two or three options. So one was to remain, to remain in Srebrenica; some could return to Bratunac, those who went from Bratunac to Srebrenica; or they could go wherever they wanted, which could be Tuzla, Serbia, Yugoslavia, as it was called at the time, or any other place of their choice, that everything would be done in order to enable them to go to the place of their choice. It was also stated that we should remain in contact continuously as a team, and that we should assist each other and take action in a timely manner. So I wouldn't go into any further details. I believe this to be the most important because this pertained to my responsibilities and my involvement in it. The lady across the table from me complained that there was certain problems. And I cannot be certain now whether it concerned her children or her grandchildren, but she said she had some problems involving small children whom she wished to be evacuated. Whereupon General Mladic suggested that she should take her children to the Fontana Hotel, where arrangements would be made to provide for them. Whereas, she herself should stay because she was among the first people to arrive at the meeting and she was supposed to be one of the key players in the team, in this team that was supposed to play an informative and assisting role and help the citizens who had already spent one night in the place they were gathered in and were in for another very hard day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could interrupt you for a moment. Now, before we go on, at one point you said you hadn't there when the lady was talking about the conditions. I take it that you were referring to that you hadn't been to Potocari or Srebrenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I was not in Potocari or in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you could please tell us how did the meeting end and what, if any, tasks you were given during those meetings and by whom.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: After that meeting where we were told that we should ensure some water tanks, food supplies, bread, milk, et cetera, as well as an infirmary and an ambulance, to provide for some wounded persons who were supposed to be transferred from a hospital that was attached to the Dutch Battalion and which was too small. And the infirmary was too small to accept -- to admit everybody who needed to be admitted when transferred from the hospital and who needed to continue to be treated as inpatients. The director of the infirmary needed help in order to make the infirmary operative. And we were told to provide the water and the rest. We continued to talk after the meeting was formally over in clusters in an informal exchange. And we were saying to each other that we would shoulder the burden as best we can and we will contribute as best we can to the alleviation of all these misfortunes. But after that I did not see anyone who attended that meeting again, and I think it is a great shame and I'm still sorry today that this meeting never came to anything. And it would have come to something, if we had acted as we had planned, namely if we had met together with the people in charge working to help the people from Srebrenica and us on the other side, keeping in touch with the representatives of the Dutch Battalion, coordinating work in a team spirit, as we had envisaged to do. If that had really been done, we would not have faced the tragedy of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could interrupt you for one second. Were you given any particular tasks?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, the general told me personally that it was a job for the civilian authorities. He saw me as the most responsible among them, and everybody continued in their line of work. We put to work everybody to make the arrangements, we organised the water tanks and the food supplies, because I suppose the shops were empty in Bratunac, and food was lacking for a great number of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we go on -- Mr. Simic, I'm going to ask very concrete questions, if you could give some concrete answers here and we'll go step by step. Were you given any specific tasks by General Mladic, and if the answer is yes, could you please tell us specifically what did General Mladic ask you or order you to do.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, the task that he assigned to me and that I was supposed to assign to all the relevant authorities was to provide food and milk for infants who were also among the people gathered in that assembly point with no roof above them, to organise an infirmary for the admission of people who were ill or wounded and who had hospital treatment in Srebrenica and were evacuated from that hospital after Srebrenica fell. And they were transferred later to the hospital of the Dutch Battalion. And those were four important tasks as far as I'm able to judge, and I wasn't even aware of the scope of my task until I arrived on the spot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could go through some of those tasks. Did you accomplish any of them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: We succeeded to the extent possible. If you consider our abilities, I think that we succeeded in the most unselfish manner. I don't want to sound as if I were boasting, but we really gave our utmost. We sent water tanks. We had one ambulance on the ground. The infirmary was reorganised and re-equipped. All the personnel that we had in the health centre was mobilised, called back to their jobs, and they were on duty in the infirmary. We increased the number of beds in the infirmary, with a contribution of the Dutch Battalion who must have been in touch with our people and who provided the things that we lacked, medicines, et cetera. All -- you have to take into account that it wasn't a real hospital; it was just an infirmary. And you know how an infirmary operates in less developed environments. We also managed to provide a certain amount of bread, water, fruit juice, and we also enjoyed in this respect great assistance of the Dutch Battalion, whose soldiers literally did manual work handling and carrying cartons like everybody on our side. There was a woman who was wounded there and who needed to be transferred to the infirmary and the ambulance was there on the spot when it was needed. And the mother of that woman was assured that they could go to the infirmary and that they would be treated just as everybody else. It was a Muslim woman. The food was a drop in the sea, I must say. I was surprised when I realised what the situation was. I had never seen anything like it. It was shocking and remains shocking to me to this day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we're going to go step by step. Before we get to your observations and further concretely speak about what you did specifically, did you contact any international organisations or work with any other internationals, other than the Dutch Battalion that were there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as I arrived and when I saw that the water was flowing in and that the infirmary was doing its work, I started concentrating on food supplies, because there was not enough food even in the Dutch Battalion. There were so many people who needed it and it required our immediate efforts. The problem was critical in Bratunac, because there were only two or three shops working in Bratunac, the local bakery baked bread for the entire population gathered there; that bread had already been distributed. So we asked for the assistance of the Zvornik bakery. And I also went to the neighbouring municipality of Ljubovija, where I had friends. I knew also my counterpart in the Ljubovija assembly and I asked him to appeal to their citizens to join in the aid operation of gathering bread and food supplies to assist the population gathered in Potocari. Ljubovija is a small and a poor place. The people responded immediately to our appeal, and they brought whatever they had. It was all collected in one spot, and we wanted to avoid any suspicion of abuse. You know how it goes in wartime. There are always stories going around about people who make a profit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can stop you for a second. Where is Ljubovija? You said it was 6 kilometres away, but where exactly is it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: On the right-hand side of the Drina, just across the river from Bratunac. You can see from one town for another. If it hadn't been for the Drina River, it would have been one town. If you could go in a straight line from one to the other, it would be just 2 kilometres if there was a bridge between the towns. It wouldn't even be 2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which country is it in?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, nowadays, it is Serbia and Montenegro. It used to be Yugoslavia. States change overnight where I come from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Other than going to Ljubovija, did you contact any international agencies or organisations for assistance?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I started talking about. We realised very soon that the abilities of Ljubovija were very small. It was far below what we needed, and that's why I decided to call the UNHCR, which had an office in Belgrade and which I had visited several times and had the best experience in cooperating with them. They assisted the people in our lands a great deal in those times. I knew some of the staff personally and I decided to ask them to intervene, if at all possible, and provide a certain amount of dry food, dry rations, that could be distributed on the spot without cooking, something that could be consumed in the field, so to speak. I was told that I should address a request, a formal request, if I wanted an affirmative answer, and that's where the problems began. I had to address this formal request, whereas everything was literally burning under my feet. I had to deal with the Serbian representatives on one side; on the other hand I had to organise humanitarian aid and to ask them that they turn a blind eye or somehow approve it. In any case, I needed their help. I asked them to intervene, and indeed two men who were on duty understood my plea and intervened. Because Serbia had imposed an embargo against us, against imports, to Bosnia at the time. So we were not able to import even the various necessities. So I had to ensure their help, and on the side of Ljubovija I wasn't sure what connections they had with the UNHCR. A commission for refugees and displaced persons was formed on behalf of Republika Srpska, and they provided assistance to Bratunac as well. I don't know what the official name of his position was, but the man number one there was Dragan Kekic. And he also promised to intervene to the extent of his abilities. I asked him to visit Bratunac if he could and to see the people in Potocari. I don't know why, but all that help arrived too late.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I was just about to ask that. Did any help arrive by UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it arrived. I don't think I would be mistaken in saying there were five trucks, white trucks. I don't know the type. But those were the trucks that usually carried humanitarian aid to Bratunac and other places. They arrived in the evening hours when the evacuation was already underway and when the drama was far gone. And they stopped at the UNPROFOR base.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with any representatives from UNHCR when this aid came to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I met with a Russian man or maybe he just had Russian parents but lived in Belgrade and worked for the UNHCR office in Belgrade. I think his name was Andrej Kazakov. He was accompanied by a lady or a young lady perhaps I should say. She was Korean, or at least we called her Korean lady. She was with him when he arrived in Potocari and continued to accompany him later on, as you will hear maybe if you're interested. I spent the entire working day with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. About what time do you recall did they arrive?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, I never wear a watch, you see, because time means nothing where I live. Money does not have the same significance as here. If there is work to do, we do it; if no, then not. I still don't wear a watch, and I look to the sun to have an idea of the time. It was still early. It --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not so hot anymore. It was getting towards dusk. The sun had already set. The transportation vehicles were fewer and fewer, and the whole commotion of running towards the buses and trucks that were supposed to take people away had subsided. So it was closer to the evening. It could have been 5.00 or 6.00 p.m. It may be important now to determine the exact time, but at that time it didn't seem so important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before we talk, before we talk about your contacts and what you did with UNHCR, I want to move back earlier when you -- before they arrived, earlier in the day, and I want to focus your attention when you were running around and trying to get the food and organise all these events. Did you at any point in time go to Potocari that day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About what time was it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I spent there most of my time when I was needed the most. And as soon as the need subsided, I went to Ljubovija to channel the transport of aid. There were also people from Ljubovija who were supposed to bring this aid, these supplies, and who were afraid to cross the line outside their town. And I had to go there to tell them they had nothing to be afraid of and to express my gratitude.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you were in Potocari, could you please tell us specifically and concretely and very briefly what you did, you Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I did all the manual work. I distributed water. I carried this and that. People called to me from all sides. They wanted jugs of water. I had to take care of some elderly people who had been literally run over by the crowd running towards the buses. I had to check the progress, if there had been any problems at the infirmary, to deal with these problems. I had to keep in touch with the UNHCR with the commission, and when these people arrived from the UNHCR it could have been 12.00 noon, or maybe 1.00 p.m. It was very hot. At that point, this smaller vehicle arrived, usually carrying senior commanders, officers, with their escorts. I stopped and I saw General Mladic addressing me. He said: "President, did you go to Srebrenica?" And I thought to myself: Why would I go to Srebrenica in this situation? He said: "I'm going there right now. If you want to go there, you can come with me." I was in two minds for a while, but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before we talk about that incident where as I understand you went to Srebrenica at some point with General Mladic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. When this vehicle came by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before we discuss that, I still remain in Potocari and I want to ask you: Did you recognise anybody there and did you speak to anybody?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Some people knew me, whereas I didn't know them. They could have been parents of my students or some people who knew me as a fellow citizen. They called me by name and asked for a favour of this type or another. They wanted me to bring them bread or water while they stayed in line. And they were afraid they would lose their place in the queue to the buses. At one point General Mladic came to me and said it would be a good idea for me to go with the commander of the Dutch Battalion to the base where there were a lot of civilians who were in this fenced-in area holding the command and the army, the troops. I didn't think any assistance was needed there because the Dutch Battalion was in charge and it would be impolite of me to trespass on the territory of the Dutch base. I asked the commander of the Dutch Battalion if he would mind, if I would be interfering with their work if I went there and the man no problem, I could come with him and he would escort me through. So I went and we toured the area around the building which housed the factory producing batteries, at least that's what I believe. I don't know much about industry or production, and I was never interested in what was produced where. All I know is it was a big plant and it was adjusted to house the soldiers of the Dutch Battalion. The people who were there had a much better time than those who stayed outside the fence. The Dutch Battalion had provided them with running water through a hose and everybody could come up to the hose and even take a shower if they wanted to. They could wash their clothes, which is exactly what women did. They washed clothes and men sat around waiting for evacuation. When I came inside, the indoors was rather ugly and for some reason muddy. There was water on the floor, and it was difficult to walk. At one point, two or three young female students of mine came up to me, whom I had no difficulty recognising because I knew them well. They seemed glad to see me. And after exchanging the usual small talk, how I was doing and how they were doing and their families, I asked if I could help them with anything. And they said: "You would help us only by speeding up this evacuation, because all that we had suffered through in Srebrenica could be over in a couple of days." One of them told me that a part of her family had already left for Tuzla or some place like that, and that when she is reunited in her family in Tuzla, she would have a much better life than in Srebrenica. Srebrenica, she said, was hell for her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you indicated that at some point you went to Srebrenica with General Mladic. Just very, very briefly could you just tell us what you did with General Mladic when you went to Srebrenica, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: As I've told you, I agreed to come along to that I wouldn't have to explain why I didn't wish to go. So there were some other people there in this street, that main street, leading towards Srebrenica. So we entered Srebrenica. There were no people there in the town itself. We saw very few people, maybe 20 older -- elderly persons around the department store. And that there was a journalist there. Mladic came up and talked to the journalist and I remained in the car. And since this conversation with the journalist was a very brief one, he came back and he asked me where was the Banja Guber source. He had never heard of it before and he wanted me to show it to the driver so we could go to the source, to the spa. And we continued to the source. En route there we stopped at a smaller source, because there are a lot of water sources there. I remember that he sat there, took off his boots, and I saw and was surprised to see that he wore wool socks. And then he took off his socks. It was quite unusual to see in the middle of the summer. Then we continued on to the source. We stayed there for about five minutes. He took off his shoes and cooled down a bit. And then we continued on and came to a spot that had been flooded before and the road was in disrepair. So we had to clean it and ensure that we could pass on that road. We continued on to the source and we found there only two or three abandoned horses wandering around. There was a wooden hut or a house there that had been burned, and everything that was man-made was destroyed. The nature was the only thing we found there. Then we went back and I was busy with my tasks, with my affairs, and the general continued on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's pick up with the UNHCR convoy and their representatives, when they showed up sometime in the late afternoon. Could you please --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us, again very briefly, what did you do with them, if anything.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I took them to the place where the evacuation was being implemented. I showed them where there was some other residents there waiting for evacuation. I told them that I had already been once to that place. I didn't want to go again, that I would wait for them there and that they should go and say that they had arrived and that they should be given every assistance they needed so that the Dutch soldiers could assist the residents that hadn't been evacuated yet. So they went there, I waited for them. They came back and said that unfortunately they were late, that they had some difficulties en route, I'm not quite sure, and then we were wondering what to do. They suggested this humanitarian aid be turned over to the Red Cross and should it be needed, that our Red Cross should be given the task of distributing the assistance, the aid. That's what we did. And since the warehouse of our Red Cross was located in the building we normally called DC in our town, which is an abbreviation for distribution centre, we headed there. We were travelling in trucks. Andrej, myself, and the young lady were going ahead. And at the entrance, I saw for the first time Mr. Blagojevic. He was standing by the main gate with a man, and I can give you my impression about what it looked like to me and what was my impression of that meeting. I think that there was somebody with a camera there, in that compound. I couldn't tell you for sure, because I didn't really care much about journalists or about people going around with cameras. I simply considered this to be an event with which I had nothing to do. Our president of the Red Cross was informed. He normally always had some group of workers around who could load and unload the goods and distribute the aid. So he came along. And I think that Mr. Blagojevic and this Russian man talked with somebody in front of the camera. I really don't know who was taping this, whether this was a TV station or it was somebody with a private camera taping this for private purposes. So they stayed there while the unloading was going on. They asked me if they could stay overnight in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Did you have a conversation with Mr. Blagojevic when you saw him there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Naturally when passing him I greeted him and we exchanged conventional greetings. How are you doing? Are there any problems? How are things? And he basically indicated, shrugged his shoulders, and indicated that there was nothing in particular. My impression was that he looked quite fresh, as though he hadn't been there at all previously but was rather somewhere resting in the shade and simply came to take a walk there. He was quite relaxed, not showing any concern or anxiety, because I would have noticed that otherwise. So this was my impression. It looked a bit strange to me, and I was somewhat envious to see that he was not very busy, where I was running around all day long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask him where he had been to look so fresh?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: No. I was afraid it would be impolite. As I told you, I was away myself for three days, so it wasn't proper for me now to question others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever find out where he had been during that day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I never inquired, nor did I hear about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated the folks from the UNHCR wanted to express the desire of staying overnight in Bratunac. Do you know whether they did?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: They did, definitely, because I took them to the only restaurant or tavern and a small bed and breakfast which we had in town. I used to go to that place before for lunch and so on. We had quite a friendly relationship with them, and I tried to maintain that. So I invited them there. I told them that the food was good; I didn't know what the accommodation was like. It was privately owned and that we would probably find two beds there. So we went to that place, and as I expected they did have room for them. And they stayed overnight there. We had dinner there as well. We stayed up talking quite late. They were not in a hurry on one hand, and I didn't want to leave them alone. So I stayed keeping them company for quite a while, and then I went home to sleep. It had been quite a long day for me. I started early in the morning, and when we parted it was near midnight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps this may be a good time before we get into the following day. Hopefully we will -- I will complete my direct during the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will have a 30-minute break. We will resume at 20 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, before we go on to the 13th, very briefly, I want to take you back to that meeting that took place at the Hotel Fontana around 10.00 that morning. Okay?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated to us that at some point -- when I asked what tasks were given to you, you told us about receiving some tasks from General Mladic. Do you know whether those tasks were on the video footage of that meeting? Apparently the meeting was videotaped.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether the entire meeting was taped, but I know that it was taped. I saw a man with a camera there. I don't know whether they taped only the very end and the informal part of the meeting. I couldn't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you met with the Prosecutor or their representative back in March the 2nd, 1998, did they show you that video by any chance?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: They didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you provide that information to them when you gave that statement back in 1998?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Because I never received the transcript. And after that interview, I never read -- reread what I had stated back then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was the transcript -- was the transcript ever made available to you by any chance?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Only yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let me fast forward now and let's get to -- incidentally, did you read your statement yesterday, the one that you gave to the Prosecution back in 1998?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I did read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And incidentally, did they ever come to ask you any further questions, say in 1999, 2000, 2001, 2002, 2003, or 2004? Did they ever come to ask you for any additional information, given the position that you held and the activities that you were involved in during that -- those critical days after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I was notified to come to Banja Luka. I couldn't tell you exactly which month it was, and I also remember that on the day of my family's patron saint, I was invited by an investigator -- I was called by either an investigator or the Prosecutor and told that there was no need for me to come, that they didn't need to talk to me. That was what was stated in the letter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the statement that you read yesterday that was provided to you for the first time, which is when we received the B/C/S version incidentally, did you notice anywhere where you discuss seeing Mr. Blagojevic by that -- in that location in that afternoon of the 12th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I think that I mentioned him, just like I did today, as standing by the entrance of the DC building. If I omitted that, then it was by accident. I'm -- I would need to take a look at it now. I couldn't claim with any certainty, although I know for a fact that I did see him and I told you what triggered that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's move to the next day, which would be July 13th, 1995. Now, on that particular day, how did it start?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I was a bit late for work that day, which was unusual for me. But I was late probably because I was very tired. I believe that most of the work had been completed and that I had nothing further to do in that respect. I came to the municipal building. I found the president of the Executive Board in his office. I stopped by to see him. He told me something that I heard for the first time then and there, which is that during the night some buses carrying people came to Bratunac and parked from the school all the way up to the stadium, including the stadium. He couldn't tell me how many buses there were there, but he told me that the buses had come during the night, that they remained there, and that in the morning hours, the buses were leaving heading towards Konjevic Polje. It was quite shocking for me to hear that. That was unexpected. I did not expect that something like that would happen. Not once was it mentioned that anyone, any convoys, were supposed to stop in Bratunac. Especially since it 10 was done during the night, and there were no able-bodied men in town, because all of them had been mobilised into the army. There were also no police, at least I didn't see any in the streets, and I don’t think they were in the station either, so I was truly shocked by this. I asked him whether he had done anything and what ought to be done about that, who should we go to see to intervene to ensure that this was removed, that these people who had been brought there are evacuated as soon as possible. I didn't know the reason why these people had been brought there. He told me that perhaps it would be a good idea to go to the Fontana Hotel because there was probably somebody on duty there or to the SDS office where I could find a duty officer with whom I could inquire with somebody about this. I naturally did this --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for a second. Why didn't you ask him why he didn't go to check out the situation at the Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So did you go to the Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I first went to the SDS office because it was closer. So I thought perhaps I should check there first and then I could continue on to the other place. I saw an officer there, a senior officer, whom I know now -- for whom I know now is called Beara. At the time I didn't know his name. I was quite upset about what had been done. As the president of the Executive Board told me, the minors had been mobilised during the night, minors who had no military experience who were used to provide security for the buses. And this was completely outrageous. I asked that these people be evacuated urgently and said that if any food or anything else was needed - and in the meantime the president of the Executive Board told me that he had contacted the Red Cross to provide all these things for these people - so I asked for that. After these supplies were unloaded, the president of the Red Cross was informed about why these supplies were needed and was told to distribute them where necessary. So following that, the evacuation of these people started. They were evacuated towards Konjevic Polje along the same route that was used the previous day for evacuation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me stop you here. Why did you go to the SDS office since you were one of the highest officials in the government? Why did you go there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: The president of the Executive Board told me that there might be a duty officer in that place. That was the only place where we could find the duty officer. And the other place was the Fontana Hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you -- how did Colonel Beara respond to your remarks?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Quite confused and I would say uninterested, which upset me even more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: So I went back and conveyed to the president of the Executive Board that we should find Miroslav because he was in charge of civilian affairs. I said that we should have Miroslav protest and say that unless things were done as promised, that we would intervene. And I think that he did convey that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you say "Miroslav," you're speaking of Mr. Deronjic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by that point in time, had you been aware of any particular position that he had been given?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: At that meeting I heard him say in front of everyone that he was in charge of civilian affairs, that he was appointed to that post by the president and that he was basically supposed to supervise the state of affairs in the civilian sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, did you have a meeting or did you run into Mr. Deronjic after this encounter with Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I did not. Because he had probably contacted him earlier, talked to him about resolving this, and I didn't really know enough about these things. I didn't know what was his task. I didn't know what exactly the president had charged him with, so I didn't know enough details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you do anything else that day that is of any significance that we might be interested in hearing about?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I had nothing else to do in Potocari in that place, because the Red Cross was in action there. Andrej told me that should the evacuation continue in -- at the same rate as previous day, that it could be finished by the afternoon. So I stopped by the health centre to see what the situation there was, and I was quite afraid that there might be some discontent leading to certain incidents and so on because there were wounded there. And I ensured that the place was secured by people who had good reputation in the community. So I hoped that this would deter any incidents. They knew that they should not let anybody in, except for the authorised personnel. Later on, I saw the Dutch Battalion doctor there. He was quite active there, also providing medical assistance, medications, some technical equipment to ensure that things were done in a proper way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you indicated that the Red Cross was in action. Did you actually see them in action or was this an assumption that you had made based on your conversations with the UNHCR representative, Andrej?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: The president of the Executive Board told me that in the morning, that they had already taken certain steps to calm down the situation, to deal with hunger, thirst, the anxiety of people who were at risk of doing something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to Potocari that day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on that particular day something happened in Kravica, the Kravica warehouse. Did you ever become aware of that incident?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I heard about that the following day, not the day when it happened. And the story that I heard was that a policeman who was guarding those people in Oka and I don't know how they came to be there, whether they were brought or they had come on their own, that that policeman was killed and then shooting ensued. And that these people had been killed, I learned later from the men returning home from the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But did you in your capacity go to visit that area to see what might have happened?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. It was not advisable for civilians to use that road, to go that way. It was said to be unsafe because armed people could come from among the trees, could emerge from the forest and shoot, and I could not make anyone drive me there. The police in the army were there and it was not my job to go. I don't know. I can't say what I could have done even if I could go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you learned of the Kravica warehouse incident, did you have any discussions with any other members of the government or the SDS president, also the commissioner, by now, of civilian affairs, Miroslav Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I asked him why that had happened and whether it could have been avoided. He seemed equally shocked and taken aback. He seemed to have heard about the incident when it was already too late for anything to be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we know from the testimony that we've heard so far that there were buses and trucks and men in -- Muslim men in those buses and trucks in the Vuk Karadzic school and elsewhere on the night of the 13th. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Karnavas, maybe you could break up your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Not a problem, Your Honour. Not a problem. It was leading in nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the afternoon of the 13th, did you become aware of anything that was happening in the town, if anything indeed was happening?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Was that the second day of evacuation?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that would be the second day of the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Apart from what I already told you about the convoy of people in buses heading towards the stadium, I didn't hear anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to switch to another topic, unless you want to supplement with any comments with respect to the second day, the 13th, or anything thereafter that you think might be relevant to this case. Okay. Now, prior to -- well, the Prosecution has argued that this was a forcible transfer, that the folks in Potocari were forced to get on the buses and to be -- and were forced to leave the area. From your observations, could you please tell us whether in your opinion they were being forced to get on those buses.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: What I saw would seem to indicate the opposite. Those people were leaving -- I don't know exactly how to put it, but they were racing each other to the bus, leaving behind their family who were infirm and who couldn't move fast enough. I had to help them to the buses. I did not have the impression that anybody was forcing anyone on to the buses. And up to the very end, I didn't see anybody being driven at gunpoint. And from talking to my female students, as I told you, I heard that they regretted not having been able to leave Srebrenica much earlier. Life there had been very difficult for some time, and many people wished for a way out of that situation. The number of people there, that I realised only then was so great, had to lead a very difficult life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said that your students had expressed a wish to having to been able to leave earlier. Had you in your capacity been engaged with any international figures or authorities in trying to make arrangements for the Muslims of Srebrenica to leave and for Serbs to come back during this period of time when the war was going on?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: In 1992 I believe we missed the chance to save the people in our area from tragedy. We were supposed to hold a meeting somewhere outside of Potocari with the authorities of Srebrenica and their army to agree on a cease-fire, on a cessation of hostilities, to reach an agreement, make it public, and ensure that no action was taken on either side to provoke the other side. However, the key man - at least in our belief he was the key man - failed to come to that meeting. He was said to hold all the strings in Srebrenica. He commanded the army or the units around Srebrenica. And that was Naser Oric. Without his presence and without his voice, we couldn't do anything. We had the impression that somebody above us did not want him to attend. That was a message from Sarajevo and that was one chance that we missed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I could --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: There was another situation, however --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before we get to the other situation, I want to concentrate on your dealings with a particular individual from the international community that was there during that period of time, 1992 or 1993, when efforts were being made to find some sort of a solution. Do you know who I'm speaking about?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: That's exactly the person I meant, General Morillon and his entry into Srebrenica. I was there in an informal capacity when General Morillon talked to some representatives of the staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. You surely know about that meeting. I should not recount it to you. Those talks presented an opportunity to find a way out rather than let the status quo continue. These talks took place at the border crossing at the Ljubovija bridge. I was coming back home; it was perhaps around 10.00 p.m., General Morillon noticed me. We exchanged a few words. He was amiable. I wanted to hear from him whether he had any ideas, any solutions to offer, anything he wanted to suggest we do to avoid the oncoming disaster in Srebrenica and Bratunac. So at his invitation, I came into this booth and talked to him through an interpreter. One of his questions took me aback. I even thought he was trying to taunt me. He said: "What kind of people are you, the Serbs? I am trying to help you with your ethnic cleansing and you are standing in my way." I was taken aback because that term "ethnic cleansing" was very ugly to me and I did not want to embrace it as an idea that I approve of or that I promote. But I said that since he had already lead a convoy of people out of Srebrenica - in which by the way I did not participate in any way, all I know is that the convoy had passed through - and an enormous number of people from Srebrenica were willing to be on that convoy and go to Tuzla. I heard from him that another convoy was in preparation, provided that an agreement was reached with the other side so that people who wanted to get out of Sarajevo could do so. However, that did not happen. After the exit of that first convoy -- and he admitted as much. I will quote him, although he used rough talk. I said: "Why are you blaming us? We made a concession. We released a number of people so the other side would do the same and release our people." I, in my job, knew that people were willing to pay thousands of Deutschmarks to help the release someone they loved from Sarajevo, from the war area, from conditions that were insufferable. And he said literally: "Somebody is screwing me here." And I said: "If that was being done to you, then what am I supposed to do?"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear quite who the general meant in his remark.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that our brigade and our officers were willing to talk to him again in search of a humane solution that needed to be found at any cost then and that we shouldn't have given up on. I still regret that it wasn't found to this day. Our brigade was not very fortunate in the choice of commanders either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Before we get to that. Before we get to that, I want to focus on this. Now, the transcript here says that Morillon, General Morillon said to you somebody was screwing him. Could you please tell us exactly what were his words and mention the person, if he mentioned anyone specifically.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: He said literally: "I was screwed by Alija Izetbegovic," he referred to the man by name. Because Alija Izetbegovic was supposed to issue his approval for the release of people from Tuzla and Sarajevo who wanted to leave these towns. These were the words he used verbatim. I remembered it very well because I pretty much liked the language he used about a serious topic like that. Since we were so impotent we could at least vent our frustration in language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know General Morillon? Did you have any personal contact with him before this encounter?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: No, no. I did not. I saw him at the Fontana Hotel when that meeting took place before the evacuation of a certain number of civilians from Srebrenica, the evacuation that he led. And he told me at that border crossing that he had a very difficult time removing a number of people who were spending the night in those trucks that were meant to take people to Tuzla and who were beating them up. And he was claiming that 90 per cent of the population of Srebrenica was willing to leave at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Incidentally, incidentally, what year is that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: It could have been the beginning of 1993 or maybe the winter of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I know it was cold. And when those convoys were on the way I was surprised there was so many people willing to be on the convoy that they accepted to spend the whole night in trucks parked in Srebrenica in order to be on them when they left for Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, prior to this period, had Serbs lived in Srebrenica or was that 100 per cent Muslim town?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Neither in Bratunac nor in Srebrenica was the population mixed at the time. It was an ethnic or a civil war, as you want to call it, and everybody wanted to have a majority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Prior to the war, had they been mixed communities?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, are you aware of any legislation, any laws, or any commissions that became in existence during that period of time that provided for the protection of the property of those leaving one area in order for them to claim the area after the civil war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as I understand it, however, you were not directly involved in implementing that law.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What do you mean I did not participate actively?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, not participate, but you were not the director or the -- of this commission, otherwise there were others who were in position to -- that implemented this law?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember when that commission was established and whether it was established by the assembly or by the War Presidency or by the Crisis Staff. If it was the assembly, then the assembly nominated the commission and set it up. And I, as an individual, was not authorised to set up any commissions without the knowledge and consent of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction in line 19 of page 38, people were willing to beat each other up to be on the transports. Nobody was being beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think that's a critical and important correction and we thank the interpreter's booth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during those days, the 12th, the 13th, other than that one encounter that you had with Mr. Blagojevic, did you see him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I hadn't seen him for a long time until one invitation that both of us received to see General Mladic in Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I'm talking about back in July.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: July, that's what I'm talking about, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, July the 12th, the 13th, the 14th, the 15th.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: After the evacuation and after learning that the majority of able-bodied men did not come to the assembly point for evacuation but instead went in the direction of Tuzla, the army went after them. So I had no opportunity to see Blagojevic. I had no idea what he did the following day, nor did I feel any need to interfere in something that was not my job and that I was not authorised to interfere with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you told us earlier that the Bratunac Brigade did not have a lot of luck with its commanders. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: They changed very often. They were replaced very often. And very frequently commanders tried to interfere in business that wasn't strictly theirs, especially civilian affairs. They blamed the municipality for everything, claimed that everything would have been much better if we allocated more food, more clothing, more cigarettes to the army, that we were to blame for all the omissions and failures. And a lot of the blame was assigned to us, although we were doing our best. So the commanders came and went, and it is true that sometimes we complained against them as well and they were replaced. But most often they replaced their own commanders. And Commander Blagojevic came to that position without our intervention. We were not even asked. I had not expected him to come to our locality. But when he did come to the brigade, it turned out that he had a decent attitude. He was simply doing his job and he did not interfere in our business, which was quite welcome. Because all we wanted was to do what we were supposed to do without mutually assigning blame.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you indicated at one time in July General Mladic asked you to meet with him, and at that occasion you met Mr. Blagojevic. My question is: Did you meet General Mladic on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. And that notification or invitation was delivered to me by the command, and they said that Commander Blagojevic was also invited. I said: "What is the purpose of this? Why am I supposed to see Mladic? Why am I supposed to go to Crna Rijeka?" And I could see that they knew nothing about it. And indeed we did not find out the purpose of our going there until we arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm not interested in all the details of the meeting. The Prosecutor may want to ask you these questions. But when you went there and when you attended this meeting, did it have anything to do Srebrenica, Potocari, or any of the events surrounding those incidents?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: No. None.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, have you heard what has happened after the fall of Srebrenica to many of the Muslim men that were either captured or surrendered or separated?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I heard as many of these stories as anybody in Bratunac, but I don't want to repeat any hearsay. It is a fact regrettably that a lot of people unnecessarily suffered and perished. But we were not able to do anything at the time. I don't want to recount any hearsay. I am willing and able to tell you what I saw, what I heard, what I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us how you feel about what you heard, you as a Serb, as a member of the government there in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Then and today I feel absolutely the same. I feel ashamed. What somebody had done brought no good to either us or the Bosnian people. And from a nation, from a people, who had every right to be proud of themselves, we were turned into a people who have to suffer shame. And the Bosnians ended up as they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after all these years of what you heard, what you saw, what you participated in, did at any point in time you hear anything about Mr. Blagojevic being directly or indirectly involved in any of these activities?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Never once. Not from a single person did I ever hear a single word that would link him up with the events. I never heard such a thing. I'm not claiming that he had nothing to do with it, but I'm claiming that I never heard this being asserted by anyone in Bratunac. There would be no reason for me to withhold the truth, had I heard something like this. But I never heard anything like this. 99 per cent of residents of Bratunac believe that Blagojevic was blamed because he was at the post of the commander of the brigade, and this is the only reason why he was ever linked with this. Otherwise, he never did anything, never took any action, and we don't think that he could prevent it. He was considered guilty without guilt. Although I said that I would not quote other people's opinions, I did do it just now, but you asked me what was the general opinion of Blagojevic and I could not withhold it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simic. I believe the Prosecutor and Mr. Stojanovic may have some questions for you. I would most appreciate it if you could be as frank and open and complete in your answers as you have been with me. Thank you very much for coming to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Mr. Stojanovic, do you have any questions to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, Your Honours, I would have just one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please. Cross-examined by Mr. Stojanovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of all your tasks and posts you held in July 1995, I would like to hear whether you had an occasion to meet Dragan Jokic ever in Bratunac or in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I heard of his name but I never met him or at least I do not remember meeting him. I have to tell you of a fault of mine. I have difficulty remembering names, numbers, and geographic terms. I heard the name Jokic mentioned. I knew that he was somewhere in the army, perhaps in Zvornik, but that's the extent of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have difficulty remembering names, but could we agree that you never saw Dragan Jokic around that time in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Even had I seen him, I wouldn't have known that this was Dragan Jokic. I told you about the officers that I did meet in those days. Had I even seen him in the street, I wouldn't have known that it was him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. We were informed that there is some technical problems, so we'll break now and give the technicians some time to do some preparations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And we'll resume at 10 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. McCloskey:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were born and raised in the Bratunac area, as you've said?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Vidoje Blagojevic was also born in the Bratunac area?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know him growing up?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: No. However, I knew his brother who was a bit younger than me and who went to the same secondary school as I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
